claim: Premature infants are highly vulnerable to aberrant gastrointestinal tract colonization.
source: Premature infants are highly vulnerable to aberrant gastrointestinal tract colonization, a process that may lead to diseases like necrotizing enterocolitis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general assertion about premature infants.

claim: Aberrant gastrointestinal tract colonization may lead to diseases like necrotizing enterocolitis.
source: Premature infants are highly vulnerable to aberrant gastrointestinal tract colonization, a process that may lead to diseases like necrotizing enterocolitis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a potential consequence of aberrant colonization.

claim: Hundreds of high-quality genomes of microorganisms that colonized co-hospitalized premature infants were reconstructed.
source: Here, we reconstructed hundreds of high-quality genomes of microorganisms that colonized co-hospitalized premature infants, assessed their metabolic potential, and tracked them over time to evaluate bacterial strain dispersal among infants.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a methodological achievement of the study.

claim: Potentially pathogenic bacteria of the same species colonized many infants.
source: Surprisingly, while potentially pathogenic bacteria of the same species colonized many infants, our genome-resolved analysis revealed that strains colonizing each baby were typically distinct.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the genome-resolved analysis.

claim: Strains colonizing each baby were typically distinct.
source: Surprisingly, while potentially pathogenic bacteria of the same species colonized many infants, our genome-resolved analysis revealed that strains colonizing each baby were typically distinct.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding from the genome-resolved analysis.

claim: No strain was common to all infants who developed necrotizing enterocolitis.
source: In particular, no strain was common to all infants who developed necrotizing enterocolitis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a specific finding regarding NEC cases.

claim: The paucity of shared gut colonizers suggests the existence of significant barriers to the spread of bacteria among infants.
source: The paucity of shared gut colonizers suggests the existence of significant barriers to the spread of bacteria among infants.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Strain-resolved comprehensive community analysis can be accomplished on potentially medically relevant time scales.
source: Importantly, we demonstrate that strain-resolved comprehensive community analysis can be accomplished on potentially medically relevant time scales.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a demonstration of the study's methodological capability.

claim: Most methods cannot distinguish between closely related strains.
source: However, the spread of bacteria among patients is hard to track because most methods cannot distinguish between closely related strains.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of existing methods.

claim: Colonization of newborns is critical for proper development.
source: Strain transmission is especially important during colonization of newborns, a process that is critical for proper development (Arrieta et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The microbiome of premature infants is often disrupted by antibiotic treatments.
source: Premature infants, in particular, are highly susceptible to aberrant colonization, as their microbiome is often disrupted by antibiotic treatments (Greenwood et al., 2014) and since the source of colonists likely includes the hospital environment (Brooks et al., 2014; Taft et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The source of colonists in premature infants likely includes the hospital environment.
source: Premature infants, in particular, are highly susceptible to aberrant colonization, as their microbiome is often disrupted by antibiotic treatments (Greenwood et al., 2014) and since the source of colonists likely includes the hospital environment (Brooks et al., 2014; Taft et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Approximately 7% of infants born weighing <1.5 kg develop NEC.
source: Recent data indicate that ∼7% of infants born weighing <1.5 kg develop NEC (Neu and Walker, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The high incidence of pneumatosis intestinalis in affected infants supports a microbial role in NEC.
source: Various observations support a microbial role in NEC, including the high incidence of pneumatosis intestinalis (gas in the bowel wall) in affected infants and resolution of symptoms in a majority of patients after antibiotic therapy and bowel rest (Grave et al., 2007; Morowitz et al., 2010; Carlisle and Morowitz, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Resolution of symptoms in a majority of NEC patients after antibiotic therapy and bowel rest supports a microbial role in NEC.
source: Various observations support a microbial role in NEC, including the high incidence of pneumatosis intestinalis (gas in the bowel wall) in affected infants and resolution of symptoms in a majority of patients after antibiotic therapy and bowel rest (Grave et al., 2007; Morowitz et al., 2010; Carlisle and Morowitz, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: NEC is characterized by intestinal inflammation and commonly progresses to necrosis, sepsis, and death.
source: NEC is characterized by intestinal inflammation and commonly progresses to necrosis, sepsis, and death.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of NEC pathology.

claim: Risk factors for NEC may include feeding with artificial infant formula, blood transfusion, infant genetics, and overall health status.
source: Risk factors may include feeding with artificial infant formula, blood transfusion, infant genetics, and overall health status (Mally et al., 2006; Schnabl et al., 2008; Neu and Walker, 2011; Wan-Huen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: NEC is commonly reported to occur in outbreaks.
source: However, NEC is commonly reported to occur in outbreaks (Boccia et al., 2001; Meinzen-Derr et al., 2009), suggesting involvement of a contagious microorganism.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The occurrence of NEC in outbreaks suggests involvement of a contagious microorganism.
source: However, NEC is commonly reported to occur in outbreaks (Boccia et al., 2001; Meinzen-Derr et al., 2009), suggesting involvement of a contagious microorganism.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from outbreak patterns.

claim: A review of 17 published outbreaks of NEC did not identify a reproducible pattern of bacterial infection.
source: A review of 17 published outbreaks of NEC did not identify a reproducible pattern of bacterial infection (Boccia et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Cultivation-based approaches to identify and track medically relevant organisms can be labor intensive, biased, and inefficient.
source: Cultivation-based approaches to identify and track medically relevant organisms can be labor intensive, biased, and inefficient.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of cultivation-based methods.

claim: Sequencing of the genomes of cultured organisms can distinguish between strains with divergent phenotypes such as antibiotic susceptibility and virulence.
source: Yet, sequencing of the genomes of these cultured organisms can distinguish between strains with divergent phenotypes such as antibiotic susceptibility and virulence (Didelot et al., 2012), and has enabled analysis of pathogen dispersal (Chin et al., 2011; Köser et al., 2012; Snitkin et al., 2012; He et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: 16S rRNA gene sequencing has limited taxonomic resolution and cannot differentiate or track distinct strains.
source: An alternative approach uses 16S rRNA gene sequencing to identify organisms without cultivation (Brooks et al., 2014; Taft et al., 2014), but the taxonomic resolution is limited, and distinct strains cannot be differentiated or tracked.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of 16S rRNA gene sequencing.

claim: Some studies using 16S rRNA gene sequencing have identified no differences between NEC cases and controls.
source: Some studies have identified no differences between cases and controls (Normann et al., 2013), while others have reported positive, but divergent findings (Wang et al., 2009; Mshvildadze et al., 2010; Mai et al., 2011; Claud et al., 2013; Morrow et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Metagenomics can profile microbial communities with strain resolution and probe the metabolic potential of community members.
source: In contrast, whole community DNA sequencing methods (metagenomics) can profile microbial communities with strain resolution and probe the metabolic potential of community members (Tyson et al., 2004; Gill et al., 2006; Kuczynski et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Metagenomics does not rely on previously established information and is less likely to miss community members compared to 16S rRNA gene surveys.
source: Unlike 16S rRNA gene surveys, metagenomics does not rely on previously established information (e.g. conserved sequences that guide PCR-based rRNA-based detection) and is less likely to miss community members (e.g. organisms with unusual rRNA sequences, phage, and plasmids).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an advantage of metagenomics.

claim: Only one small study has analyzed metagenomic sequence data from infants with and without NEC.
source: Only one small study that we are aware of has analyzed metagenomic sequence data from infants with and without NEC (Claud et al., 2013), but assembly of the sequences was not attempted.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: During the summer of 2014, nine infants were diagnosed with NEC (Bell's stage II or III).
source: Ultimately, during the summer of 2014, nine infants were diagnosed with NEC (Bell's stage II or III).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a clinical observation.

claim: The total number of NEC cases was 10, as one of the affected infants developed recurrent NEC.
source: The total number of NEC cases was 10, as one of the affected infants developed recurrent NEC.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a clinical observation.

claim: The NEC incidence rate in summer 2014 was 2.5 times higher than average for this NICU.
source: This incidence rate was 2.5 times higher than average for this NICU.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison to historical data.

claim: The estimated bacterial load was in general agreement with previous measurements in full-term infants of similar postnatal ages.
source: The estimated load was in general agreement with previous measurements in full-term infants of similar postnatal ages (De Leoz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: The variation in the number of microbes per gram feces did not exceed a 100-fold across all samples.
source: Notably, the variation in the number of microbes per gram feces did not exceed a 100-fold across all samples.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from ddPCR analysis.

claim: Infants who developed NEC did not show a consistent trend of change in bacterial load prior to or following diagnosis.
source: Infants who developed NEC did not show a consistent trend of change in bacterial load prior to or following diagnosis (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1.

claim: A total of 509 bacterial genomes were recovered.
source: A total of 509 bacterial genomes (including multiple genomes for the same organism in different samples) were recovered, with average read coverage of between 2 and 1148.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological outcome.

claim: 260 near-complete genomes were reconstructed.
source: Between 1 and 23 bacterial genome bins were detected per sample, and overall 260 near-complete genomes were reconstructed (see 'Materials and methods' section).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological outcome.

claim: Between 86% and 98% of reads generated for each sample was assigned to a genome bin.
source: Overall, between 86% and 98% of reads generated for each sample was assigned to a genome bin (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological outcome.

claim: Very few bacterial strains occurred in more than one infant.
source: Remarkably, very few bacterial strains occurred in more than one infant and no strain was shared by all infants who developed NEC (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Identical genotypes were almost always detected in samples from the same infant.
source: In contrast, and as could be expected, identical genotypes were almost always detected in samples from the same infant, providing reassurance regarding the validity of our methods (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Of the 149 strains compared, only four were shared by two or more infants.
source: Specifically, of the 149 strains compared, only four were shared by two or more infants, and only three of these were identified in infants who developed NEC.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from comparative genomic analysis.

claim: A Klebsiella oxytoca strain was present in infants #1 and #6, neither of whom developed NEC.
source: A Klebsiella oxytoca strain was present in infants #1 and #6, neither of whom developed NEC.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from strain comparison.

claim: Clostridium sporogenes was present in infants #3 and #5.
source: Clostridium sporogenes was present in infants #3 and #5, but occurred at very low abundance in infant #3.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from strain comparison.

claim: A Clostridium butyricum strain was detected in infants who did (infants #3, #8) and did not (infants #1, #5, #6) develop NEC but was missing from infant #2, who developed NEC.
source: Two strains were more widely distributed: a Clostridium butyricum strain was detected in infants who did (infants #3, #8) and did not (infants #1, #5, #6) develop NEC but was missing from infant #2, who developed NEC.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from strain comparison.

claim: C. butyricum has no predicted type III or type VI secretion system genes and no identified toxin-producing genes.
source: C. butyricum has no predicted type III or type VI secretion system genes and no identified toxin-producing genes (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from metabolic profiling.

claim: C. butyricum seems unlikely to be a pathogen or the cause of NEC.
source: Thus, this strain seems unlikely to be a pathogen or the cause of NEC.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the lack of pathogenicity genes.

claim: A Clostridium paraputrificum strain with a moderate predicted pathogenicity potential was shared by infants #2, #5, and #8.
source: Lastly, a Clostridium paraputrificum strain with a moderate predicted pathogenicity potential (Supplementary file 4) was shared by infants #2, #5, and #8, and also occurred in one sample from infant #6, although the predominant strain in this infant (who did not develop NEC) was different (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from strain comparison and metabolic profiling.

claim: C. paraputrificum was not detected in infant #3 (NEC case).
source: C. paraputrificum was not detected in infant #3 (NEC case).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from strain comparison.

claim: Both C. paraputrificum and C. butyricum have been previously suggested as potential causative agents in NEC.
source: Both C. paraputrificum and C. butyricum have been previously suggested as potential causative agents in NEC (Waligora-Dupriet et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: Multiple distinct Veillonella strains and species were present across infants.
source: Interestingly, although the colonizing strains were almost always distinct, infants often shared bacteria of the same genus or species. At high abundance in multiple infants, including two who developed NEC, were members of the genus Veillonella. However, multiple distinct strains and species were present across infants (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3.

claim: A Veillonella strain was very abundant in infant #2 prior to development of NEC but disappeared after the first antibiotic treatment.
source: A Veillonella strain was very abundant in infant #2 prior to development of NEC (Supplementary file 3) but disappeared after the first antibiotic treatment, to be replaced by different Veillonella species (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The results likely rule out a Veillonella strain as a single, shared agent of NEC.
source: The results likely rule out a Veillonella strain as a single, shared agent of NEC.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the strain diversity.

claim: Enterococcus faecalis is common in fecal samples from both premature and term infants.
source: Another organism found in multiple infants, often at high abundance (Figure 2 and Supplementary file 3), was Enterococcus faecalis. This organism is common in fecal samples from both premature and term infants (Chang et al., 2011; Costello et al., 2013; Vallès et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: E. faecalis has repeatedly been identified as a source of neonatal infection.
source: Although E. faecalis has repeatedly been identified as a source of neonatal infection (Stoll et al., 2002; Härtel et al., 2012), it also has been studied as a potential probiotic (Nueno-Palop and Narbad, 2011), with beneficial properties related to modulation of innate immunity (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: E. faecalis has been studied as a potential probiotic with beneficial properties related to modulation of innate immunity.
source: Although E. faecalis has repeatedly been identified as a source of neonatal infection (Stoll et al., 2002; Härtel et al., 2012), it also has been studied as a potential probiotic (Nueno-Palop and Narbad, 2011), with beneficial properties related to modulation of innate immunity (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: Links between mobile genomic elements and enterococcal virulence are well described.
source: Furthermore, links between mobile genomic elements and enterococcal virulence are well described (Gilmore et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: 30 near-complete E. faecalis genomes were reconstructed.
source: For E. faecalis, we reconstructed 30 near-complete genomes (Supplementary file 3) for multiple strains (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological outcome.

claim: Alignment of the E. faecalis gyrA gene illustrates five distinct sequence types.
source: Alignment of the longest of the single copy genes tracked, the ∼2500 bp DNA gyrase subunit A (gyrA) gene, illustrates five distinct sequence types for this gene alone (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Reconstructed 16S rRNA gene sequences were identical in E. faecalis strains from infants #2 and #7 and from infants #3 and #5 (early samples).
source: Notably, reconstructed 16S rRNA gene sequences were identical in these strains, illustrating that the limited taxonomic resolution of this locus prevents its use in studies of strain dispersal.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from sequence comparison.

claim: The limited taxonomic resolution of the 16S rRNA gene locus prevents its use in studies of strain dispersal.
source: Notably, reconstructed 16S rRNA gene sequences were identical in these strains, illustrating that the limited taxonomic resolution of this locus prevents its use in studies of strain dispersal.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the identical 16S rRNA sequences in distinct strains.

claim: All 30 well-sampled E. faecalis genomes encode a CRISPR spacer-repeat array that lacks proximal Cas proteins.
source: All 30 well-sampled E. faecalis genomes encode a CRISPR spacer-repeat array that lacks proximal Cas proteins and some genomes (in infants #3, #5, #8) encode an additional locus with proximal Cas genes (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4B,C.

claim: E. faecalis strains in infants #2, #6, #7, and #9 that lack Cas proteins altogether have lost CRISPR-Cas-based phage immunity.
source: Given that Cas proteins are required for CRISPR-Cas function, strains in infants #2, #6, #7, and #9 that lack Cas proteins altogether, have lost CRISPR-Cas-based phage immunity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the absence of Cas proteins.

claim: The pattern of CRISPR loci with and without Cas proteins has been reported previously in E. faecalis.
source: This pattern of loci with and without Cas proteins has been reported previously in E. faecalis (Palmer and Gilmore, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: The repeat-spacer arrays in the loci with Cas1 type a are identical in the genotypes of E. faecalis in infant #3 and in early samples from infant #5.
source: The repeat-spacer arrays in the loci with Cas1 type a are identical in the genotypes of E. faecalis in infant #3 and in early samples from infant #5 (Figure 5A), reinforcing the very high similarity of these populations deduced from single copy gene sequence comparisons (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 5A and Figure 2.

claim: A block comprising six spacers and flanking repeats has been excised in the E. faecalis strain from infant #8.
source: As often happens in CRISPR loci (Tyson and Banfield, 2008), a block comprising six spacers and flanking repeats has been excised in the strain from infant #8 and three novel spacers have been added at the growing tip, versus two in infants #3 and #5 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 5A and citation support.

claim: Shared spacers at the older end of CRISPR loci imply that the E. faecalis strains in infants #3, #5, and #8 had a recent common ancestor.
source: Shared spacers at the older end (distant from the Cas) imply that the strains in infants #3, #5, and #8 had a recent common ancestor.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from shared CRISPR spacers.

claim: The multiple alignment of E. faecalis consensus sequences revealed many SNP locations and small indels spread across the entire length of the sequence, as well as a small number of longer (20–30 Kbp) indel regions.
source: The analysis revealed many SNP locations and small indels that were spread across the entire length of the sequence, as well as a small number of longer (20–30 Kbp) indel regions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from multiple alignment analysis.

claim: On average, E. faecalis sequence pairs were ∼90% identical across the scaffold length.
source: While, on average, sequence pairs were ∼90% identical across the scaffold length, those of infants #2 and #7 and those of infants #3 and #5 (early samples) showed identity of 99.3% and 98.7%, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from sequence comparison.

claim: E. faecalis strains in infants #2 and #7 showed 99.3% identity.
source: While, on average, sequence pairs were ∼90% identical across the scaffold length, those of infants #2 and #7 and those of infants #3 and #5 (early samples) showed identity of 99.3% and 98.7%, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from sequence comparison.

claim: E. faecalis strains in infants #3 and #5 (early samples) showed 98.7% identity.
source: While, on average, sequence pairs were ∼90% identical across the scaffold length, those of infants #2 and #7 and those of infants #3 and #5 (early samples) showed identity of 99.3% and 98.7%, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from sequence comparison.

claim: A ∼1 Kbp region distinguishes E. faecalis strains in infants #3 and #5.
source: Interestingly, a ∼1 Kbp region distinguishes strains in infants #3 and #5 (Figure 6C), whereas a prophage insertion separates those in infants #2 and #7 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: A prophage insertion separates E. faecalis strains in infants #2 and #7.
source: Interestingly, a ∼1 Kbp region distinguishes strains in infants #3 and #5 (Figure 6C), whereas a prophage insertion separates those in infants #2 and #7 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 6D.

claim: The prophage insertion difference between E. faecalis strains in infants #2 and #7 might have arisen after colonization.
source: These differences are very subtle, and especially in the case of the prophage, might have arisen after colonization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as speculation about the timing of the prophage insertion.

claim: In infant #3, ∼0.12% of E. faecalis reads have sequences consistent with derivation from the genotype in infants #2 and #7.
source: However, in infant #3, ∼0.12% of reads have sequences consistent with derivation from the genotype in infants #2 and #7, which are indistinguishable at this locus (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from read polymorphism analysis.

claim: The E. faecalis genotype from infants #2 and #7 is present at 3–9% in early-collected samples from infant #5.
source: The gyrA analysis indicated that this genome is even more prominent in early-collected samples from infant #5 (3–9% of reads; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from gyrA analysis.

claim: The E. faecalis population in infants #2 and #7 is relatively widely distributed compared to other E. faecalis strains.
source: Thus, compared to other E. faecalis strains, the population in infants #2 and #7 is relatively widely distributed.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the detection of this strain in other infants.

claim: Multiple E. faecalis inoculation events occur during colonization.
source: This, and the detection of the dominant strain from infants #2 and #7 in other infants indicate that multiple E. faecalis inoculation events occur during colonization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the detection of multiple strains.

claim: The lack of overlap in E. faecalis strain genotype could indicate the existence of infant-specific strain sources and barriers that prevent spread of those populations to other infants in the NICU.
source: The lack of overlap in strain genotype could indicate the existence of infant-specific strain sources (e.g. mothers), and barriers that prevent spread of those populations to other infants in the NICU.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as speculation about the cause of strain specificity.

claim: The founding E. faecalis population may preclude establishment of later introduced populations.
source: Even if dispersal occurs, the founding population may preclude establishment of later introduced populations.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as speculation about colonization dynamics.

claim: Strain dominance could reflect strong selection in the gastrointestinal tract leading to the establishment of a single, most adapted strain.
source: Alternatively, strains could be dispersing freely, and strain dominance could reflect strong selection in the gastrointestinal tract (possibly imposed by microbial community context and/or human genetics) leading to the establishment of a single, most adapted strain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as speculation about colonization dynamics.

claim: Previous studies have pointed to a high abundance of Proteobacteria as a factor in NEC development.
source: Previous studies that were done at lower resolution than achieved in the current study have pointed to a high abundance of Proteobacteria as a factor in NEC development (Wang et al., 2009; Mai et al., 2011; Torrazza et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: Proteobacteria representation in the communities did not distinguish those infants who developed NEC from those that did not.
source: Proteobacteria are abundant in most infants, but Proteobacteria representation in the communities did not distinguish those infants who developed NEC from those that did not.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from phylum-level analysis.

claim: The relative abundance of Proteobacteria declines in infant #2 prior to both NEC diagnoses.
source: In fact, the relative abundance of Proteobacteria declines in infant #2 prior to both NEC diagnoses.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from phylum-level analysis.

claim: Clustering analyses of the detailed profiles of genomically encoded metabolic capacities failed to distinguish the capacities of microbial communities in infants who did and did not develop NEC.
source: However, clustering analyses of the detailed profiles of genomically encoded metabolic capacities (Supplementary file 4) and inspection of individual patterns failed to distinguish the capacities of microbial communities in infants who did and did not develop NEC.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from metabolic profiling.

claim: Many pathogens were detected in fecal samples of infants who developed NEC.
source: While no metabolic imbalance was found, many pathogens were detected in fecal samples of infants who developed NEC.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from metabolic profiling.

claim: Enterobacter cloacae is abundant in infant #2 and is predicted to have many toxin and type VI secretion system genes and an extensive antibiotic resistance repertoire.
source: For example, Enterobacter cloacae is abundant in infant #2 and is predicted to have many toxin and type VI secretion system genes and an extensive antibiotic resistance repertoire (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from metabolic profiling.

claim: The antibiotic resistance genes in E. cloacae may explain why it remained abundant after antibiotic treatment.
source: The resistance genes may explain why E. cloacae remained abundant after antibiotic treatment (sequence analyses indicate that the same genotype persisted through the treatments; Figure 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the persistence of E. cloacae and its antibiotic resistance genes.

claim: C. difficile has been implicated as a cause of NEC.
source: C. difficile has been implicated as a cause of NEC (Han et al., 1983; Pérez-González et al., 1996), although its role is controversial (Boccia et al., 2001; Mshvildadze et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: The genome of C. difficile in infant #2 encodes tcdABCDE genes characteristic of toxigenic strains.
source: Notably, the genome of the organism in infant #2 encodes tcdABCDE genes characteristic of toxigenic strains (Dingle et al., 2014) and Clostridial binary toxin B/anthrax toxin PA family proteins are affiliated with this organism.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from metabolic profiling with citation support.

claim: Bifidobacterium (MSTE12-related) is not frequently observed in premature infants.
source: Interestingly, the communities in infant #3 included Bifidobacterium (MSTE12-related), an organism that is often considered to be a beneficial commensal and not frequently observed in premature infants (Butel et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: Infants who were not diagnosed with NEC were likewise colonized by a wide variety of potentially pathogenic bacteria.
source: Infants who were not diagnosed with NEC were likewise colonized by a wide variety of potentially pathogenic bacteria and some strains were even shared by NEC cases and controls.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from metabolic profiling.

claim: If gut colonization by pathogenic bacteria is a significant factor in the development of NEC, other health and/or environmental attributes may ultimately determine which infants become sick.
source: If gut colonization by pathogenic bacteria is a significant factor in the development of NEC, other health and/or environmental attributes may ultimately determine which infants become sick.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as speculation about NEC etiology.

claim: No mobile elements were shared by all sick infants, or by all infants diagnosed with NEC.
source: However, no mobile elements were shared by all sick infants, or by all infants diagnosed with NEC (see 'Materials and methods' section).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from mobile element comparison.

claim: No E. faecalis CRISPR spacer with a perfect match to any phage that coexisted in the same community was identified.
source: In no case did we identify an E. faecalis CRISPR spacer with a perfect match to any phage that coexisted in the same community (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from CRISPR-phage analysis.

claim: Imperfect matches between E. faecalis CRISPR spacers and phage in the same sample were detected.
source: However, we detected imperfect matches between E. faecalis CRISPR spacers and phage in the same sample, and some spacers matched perfectly to phage in other samples from the same infant and to phage in another infant.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from CRISPR-phage analysis.

claim: One spacer in the CRISPR locus of E. faecalis from infant #3 targets a prophage integrated into the genome of E. faecalis from infant #5.
source: One spacer in the CRISPR locus of E. faecalis from infant #3 targets a prophage integrated into the genome of E. faecalis from infant #5 (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from CRISPR-phage analysis.

claim: The observations indicate recent exposure of E. faecalis to phage populations related to those that coexisted in the NICU during the study period.
source: These observations indicate recent exposure of E. faecalis to phage populations related to those that coexisted in the NICU during the study period and suggest phage sensitivity of bacterial populations in this early gut colonization period.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from CRISPR-phage analysis.

claim: Enterobacteriales phage genomes were 95× and 30× more abundant than the genome of the probable Klebsiella host in samples 2 and 3 from infant #1.
source: Notable in samples 2 and 3 from infant #1 were Enterobacteriales phage, the genomes of which were 95× and 30× more abundant than the genome of the probable Klebsiella host (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from phage abundance analysis.

claim: The period of phage proliferation in infant #1 corresponded to an increase in overall cell numbers by a factor of 10 over ∼5 days.
source: Interestingly, ddPCR shows that the period of phage proliferation corresponded to an increase in overall cell numbers by a factor of 10 over ∼5 days (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1.

claim: K. oxytoca must account for the increase in bacterial cell numbers in infant #1 because it is essentially the only species in early-sampled communities.
source: K. oxytoca must account for this increase in bacterial cell numbers because it is essentially the only species in early-sampled communities.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from community composition.

claim: Phage predation moderated the Klebsiella bloom and probably facilitated the subsequent establishment of the more complex community in later-collected samples from infant #1.
source: We infer that phage predation moderated the Klebsiella bloom and probably facilitated the subsequent establishment of the more complex community in later-collected samples.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from phage abundance and community dynamics.

claim: No seasonal or otherwise periodic patterns in NEC diagnoses were observed.
source: No seasonal or otherwise periodic patterns in NEC diagnoses were observed, and no correlation between the number of NEC cases and daily average of hospitalized infants in the NICU was detected.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from statistical analysis.

claim: No correlation between the number of NEC cases and daily average of hospitalized infants in the NICU was detected.
source: No seasonal or otherwise periodic patterns in NEC diagnoses were observed, and no correlation between the number of NEC cases and daily average of hospitalized infants in the NICU was detected.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from statistical analysis.

claim: Data were somewhat over-dispersed relative to the Poisson distribution.
source: Data were somewhat over-dispersed relative to the Poisson distribution (Figure 9B) and fit the negative binomial distribution modestly better (R2 = 0.85 for Poisson model, R2 = 0.95 for NB model), in line with a potential dependency between diagnosed cases.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 9B.

claim: The eight NEC cases from summer 2014 that met VON criteria could not be established as statistically significant, assuming Poisson or negative binomial distributions.
source: While the eight cases from summer 2014 that met VON criteria are undoubtedly at the high end of the scale, they could not be established as statistically significant, assuming these underlying Poisson or NB distributions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from statistical analysis.

claim: Two near-complete Veillonella genomes (>4 Mbp) were assembled into 12 and 15 pieces.
source: For example, two near-complete Veillonella genomes (>4 Mbp) were assembled into 12 and 15 pieces, four E. faecalis genomes were reconstructed into 27–43 pieces, two Actinomyces into 21 and 24 pieces, one Negativicoccus succinicivorans genome into 12 pieces, and one Citrobacter strain genome into 23 pieces.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological outcome.

claim: An ∼12.7 Mbp draft genome of C. parapsilosis was reconstructed.
source: Interestingly, we reconstructed an ∼12.7 Mbp draft genome of C. parapsilosis, a microbial eukaryote (fungus) that was highly abundant in the gut of infant #9 after treatment for NEC (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 10A.

claim: The C. parapsilosis genome shares >99% identity with the genome of the CDC317 isolate.
source: The genome shares >99% identity with the genome of the CDC317 isolate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from genome comparison.

claim: Very few microbial eukaryote genomes have been recovered previously from metagenomic data.
source: Alignment of our genome with the CDC317 genome verified the overall accuracy of our assembly, a notable finding given that very few microbial eukaryote genomes have been recovered previously from metagenomic data (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as context for the C. parapsilosis genome reconstruction.

claim: An organism whose 16S rRNA gene sequence shares 99% identity with Streptococcus agalactiae (group B streptococcus, GBS) was identified in samples 4 and 5 from infant #1.
source: Although present at very low abundance (∼0.2%), we identified an organism whose 16S rRNA gene sequence shares 99% identity with Streptococcus agalactiae (group B streptococcus, GBS), in samples 4 and 5 (Figure 10B and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 10B and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The infant #1's mother tested positive on her GBS surveillance swab.
source: The infant's mother tested positive on her GBS surveillance swab and the placenta was found by pathologists to contain trace amounts of GBS.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as clinical information.

claim: The newborn blood culture from infant #1 was negative for GBS.
source: However, the newborn blood culture was negative for GBS.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as clinical information.

claim: The GBS organism likely caused the episode of early onset sepsis in infant #1.
source: Likely, this organism caused the episode of early onset sepsis in this infant.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the detection of GBS and clinical context.

claim: The time between collection of the last fecal sample and receipt of DNA sequence information from all 55 samples was 10 days.
source: The time between collection of the last fecal sample and receipt of DNA sequence information from all 55 samples was 10 days.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological outcome.

claim: For a group of three samples, the time required for DNA extraction is a couple of hours and for sequencing, about 2 days.
source: For a group of three samples, as might be collected in a clinical setting, the time required for DNA extraction is a couple of hours and for sequencing, about 2 days (the sequencing speed is method dependent).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological outcome.

claim: Sequence assembly, annotation, and data import into the metagenomics analysis system required 6–8 hr/sample.
source: Sequence assembly, annotation, and data import into our metagenomics analysis system required 6–8 hr/sample and the time required for a first round binning that largely defined community composition and metabolic potential (generated automatically) was ∼10 to ∼60 min/sample.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological outcome.

claim: The time required for a first round binning was ∼10 to ∼60 min/sample.
source: Sequence assembly, annotation, and data import into our metagenomics analysis system required 6–8 hr/sample and the time required for a first round binning that largely defined community composition and metabolic potential (generated automatically) was ∼10 to ∼60 min/sample.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological outcome.

claim: New bioinformatics approaches enable comprehensive genome-based analyses on a timescale that approaches that required for some clinical applications.
source: Thus, new bioinformatics approaches tested here enable comprehensive genome-based analyses on a timescale that approaches that required for some clinical applications, for example involving patients with long-term health issues.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the methodological outcomes.

claim: All microbial communities in all infants sampled prior to onset of NEC harbored organisms with significant pathogenicity potential.
source: All microbial communities in all infants sampled prior to onset of NEC harbored organisms with significant pathogenicity potential.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a summary finding.

claim: No evidence for one common, abundant (or even minor) genomically distinct infective agent was found.
source: However, we found no evidence for one common, abundant (or even minor) genomically distinct infective agent.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a summary finding.

claim: If bacteria contribute to NEC, the effect more likely is due to exposure to a variety of potentially dangerous hospital-associated bacteria.
source: If bacteria contribute to NEC, the effect more likely is due to exposure to a variety of potentially dangerous hospital-associated bacteria.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The dominant population of each bacterium acquired by each infant was generally genotypically distinct.
source: A major finding is that the dominant population of each bacterium acquired by each infant was generally genotypically distinct.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a summary finding.

claim: Extremely closely related organisms were only identified in a handful of cases, and occurred in both sick and healthy infants.
source: Extremely closely related organisms were only identified in a handful of cases, and occurred in both sick and healthy infants.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a summary finding.

claim: Dispersal can occur among infants in the NICU.
source: Yet, the fact that they were identified at all, and the detection of shared minor strains of E. faecalis in a few cases, confirms that dispersal can occur among infants in the NICU.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as an inference from the detection of shared strains.

claim: Significant barriers exist that limit establishment of strains during the early stages of colonization of the premature infant gastrointestinal tract.
source: Overall, we suspect the existence of significant barriers that limit establishment of strains during the early stages of colonization of the premature infant gastrointestinal tract.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Between 2.22 and 7.35 Gbp of trimmed data from each sample was assembled independently.
source: Between 2.22 and 7.35 Gbp of trimmed data from each sample was assembled independently.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological detail.

claim: In total, 1.35 Gbp of genome sequence was generated on scaffolds >1000 bp.
source: In total, 1.35 Gbp of genome sequence was generated on scaffolds >1000 bp (see 'Materials and methods' section and Supplementary files 2 and 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological outcome.

claim: Genome bins with >0.5 Mbp of sequence were compared by aligning the single copy genes sequences.
source: In order to assess the extent of strain dispersal among the hospitalized infants, genome bins with >0.5 Mbp of sequence were compared by aligning the single copy genes sequences.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological detail.

claim: Genome bins that were >98% identical across >90% of bin length were considered indistinguishable.
source: Genome bins that were >98% identical across >90% of bin length were considered indistinguishable.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological detail.
